title: Computational Complexity for Data Science
text:
Computational complexity asks how much time, memory or randomness a problem needs, whatever algorithm solves it. Data science meets it whenever fitting a model exactly turns out to be computationally hard, which is one reason practical methods use greedy search or a convex surrogate loss.
These notes collect the computational complexity that data science courses use. They are new. The pages written so far are:

Asymptotic notation: big-O, big-Omega and big-Theta, and what it means for a computation to cost \(O(D)\)

The planned topics still to come are:

models of computation: Turing machines and computability
time and space complexity, and the classes P and NP
reductions and NP-completeness
randomized computation
communication and information complexity

Information theory has its own library, Information Theory for Data Science. Results that connect the two live in the library that holds their main statement, and the other links to them.

title: Computational Complexity for Data Science
text:
Starting materials
These notes are written fresh, but they draw on the following books and Stanford course pages.

Sanjeev Arora and Boaz Barak, Computational Complexity: A Modern Approach, the main starting point for complexity theory.
CS154: Introduction to the Theory of Computation (Omer Reingold and Li-Yang Tan), which covers automata, computability and complexity, using Michael Sipser’s Introduction to the Theory of Computation, with lecture slides and videos.
CS154: Introduction to Automata and Complexity Theory (Spring 2009, with Rajeev Motwani among the course staff), with handouts, homework and a reading list.
Introduction to Automata Theory, Languages, and Computation, Jeff Ullman’s home page for the book, which is the textbook the 2009 CS154 page links. It has solutions to starred exercises, errata, slides, and past CS154 course materials.
CS254: Computational Complexity (Li-Yang Tan), which covers space complexity, the polynomial hierarchy, randomized and non-uniform computation, and interactive proofs. It uses Arora and Barak and Avi Wigderson’s Mathematics and Computation, and links a reading for each lecture.

section: Using these notes in another site
text:
Using these notes in another site
Course sites link to these pages by URL; they do not include this repository as a git submodule. A host site that keeps a copy of this repository at its root, named cds, can still include fragments with paths that start with cds/. This site includes its own fragments the same way, through a cds symlink that points at the repository root.
Quarto resolves @id cross-references only within one rendered page, so a host site that links to a result here uses an explicit link to the page and anchor.

title: Asymptotic notation
text: The cost of an algorithm depends on the size \(n\) of its input. Asymptotic notation compares how two costs grow as \(n\) grows, ignoring constant factors and small inputs.

title: Asymptotic notation
text:
1 Upper, lower and tight bounds








Definition 1 (Big-O notation) Let \(f\) and \(g\) be functions from the positive integers to \([0, \infty)\). We write \(f(n) = O(g(n))\) if there are a constant \(c > 0\) and an integer \(n_0\) such that
\[f(n) \le c \, g(n) \quad \text{for every } n \ge n_0.\]
That is, \(f\) grows no faster than a constant multiple of \(g\) once \(n\) is large enough. This is the definition of Arora and Barak (2009, sec. 0.3).











Definition 2 (Big-Omega notation) For \(f\) and \(g\) as in Definition 1, we write \(f(n) = \Omega(g(n))\) if there are a constant \(c > 0\) and an integer \(n_0\) such that
\[f(n) \ge c \, g(n) \quad \text{for every } n \ge n_0.\]
Dividing by \(c\) shows that this holds exactly when \(g(n) = O(f(n))\), with constant \(1/c\).











Definition 3 (Big-Theta notation) For \(f\) and \(g\) as in Definition 1, we write \(f(n) = \Theta(g(n))\) if both \(f(n) = O(g(n))\) (Definition 1) and \(f(n) = \Omega(g(n))\) (Definition 2). Then \(f\) and \(g\) grow at the same rate, up to constant factors.











Remark 1 (The equals sign is one-way). \(O(g(n))\) stands for a set of functions, and \(f(n) = O(g(n))\) says that \(f\) belongs to it. So \(n = O(n^2)\) is true, but \(n^2 = O(n)\) is false, and the statement cannot be read from right to left. Cormen et al. (2009, sec. 3.1) reads the notation this way.

title: Asymptotic notation
text:
2 Examples








Example 1 (A quadratic is \(O(n^2)\) but not \(O(n)\)) Let \(f(n) = 3n^2 + 5n\).
For \(n \ge 5\), we have \(5n \le n \cdot n = n^2\), so
\[
\begin{aligned}
f(n)
&= 3n^2 + 5n \\
&\le 3n^2 + n^2 \\
&= 4n^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
So \(f(n) = O(n^2)\), with \(c = 4\) and \(n_0 = 5\) in Definition 1. Since \(f(n) \ge 3n^2\) for every \(n\), also \(f(n) = \Omega(n^2)\) (Definition 2), and so \(f(n) = \Theta(n^2)\) (Definition 3).
But \(f(n)\) is not \(O(n)\). If it were, there would be \(c > 0\) and \(n_0\) with \(3n^2 + 5n \le c \, n\) for every \(n \ge n_0\). Dividing both sides by \(n > 0\) gives \(3n + 5 \le c\) for every \(n \ge n_0\), which fails for any \(n\) larger than both \(n_0\) and \((c - 5)/3\).











Example 2 (Counting the operations in an inner product) The inner product of two vectors \(\tilde{x}, \tilde{z}\in \mathbb{R}^D\) is
\[\tilde{x}^\top \tilde{z}= x_1 z_1 + x_2 z_2 + \cdots + x_D z_D.\]
Computing it takes \(D\) multiplications, one for each product \(x_d z_d\), and \(D - 1\) additions to sum the \(D\) products: \(2D - 1\) arithmetic operations in all. Since \(2D - 1 \le 2D\) for every \(D \ge 1\), the cost is \(O(D)\), with \(D\) in the role of \(n\), \(c = 2\) and \(n_0 = 1\) in Definition 1. Since \(2D - 1 \ge D\) for every \(D \ge 1\), it is also \(\Omega(D)\) (Definition 2), so it is \(\Theta(D)\) (Definition 3). When a machine learning text says an inner product “costs \(O(D)\)”, it means this count of operations, up to a constant factor.
